From one week's chain to the week that breaks the floor

This page shows how the skill forecasts the money in your bank, one level at a time. It starts with one week of cash in and cash out. It ends with a forecast that rolls forward after a week of real receipts. The page quotes every rule from the skill itself. It also works every number in front of you.

How it thinks

Fourteen rules the whole skill runs on

Every level below applies one or more of these rules. The examples use one company, Northbrook Trading, and one forecast of 13 weeks from Monday 6 October. Its floor is a covenant of $150,000, measured on cash net of restricted cash. Its opening available cash is $182,400: the Operating account at $151,900 plus the Savings account at $30,500. The Tax Reserve account holds $24,000 of restricted cash, so the skill leaves it out. The two figures are the bank balances on 6 October. The skill agrees them to the books through the latest bank reconciliation.

Learning path

Six levels, from simple to complex

Check it yourself

Put in your own 13 weeks

Enter your opening cash, your floor, and the receipts and disbursements you expect in each week. Or load the Northbrook example. The page runs the chain week by week and finds the lowest point, the headroom and the runway. The page sends nothing anywhere.

The starting point

Leave the floor empty if you have none. The page then tests only the weeks below zero.

Each week, as you expect it to hit the bank
WeekReceipts inDisbursements out

Each week the page computes closing = opening + receipts − disbursements, and the next week opens at that closing. Headroom is closing − floor. The runway is the first week whose closing is below zero, or "not within the horizon". The page says "ties" when the sum of the 13 weekly net flows equals closing cash in week 13 minus opening cash in week 1. The "Northbrook, October" preset is the grid used in every level above.

Using it

What it asks, needs and gives back

Asks firstDo you want to use MosoFin for this run, or upload the data yourself? What horizon, from which start date? Which accounts count as available cash, and is any cash restricted? What is your payroll calendar: pay dates, net pay, tax remittance dates and benefit dates? Which debt payments, tax due dates and other large one-off payments fall inside the horizon? Which open bills do you plan to pay, and when? What is your minimum cash floor, is it a covenant or your own preference, and how does it define cash? Do you have a credit facility? Is cash pooled between your companies? On the MosoFin path, it also asks for the bank balance of each account on the start date.
NeedsThe skill needs the bank balance of each account on the start date, with restricted accounts marked, and the latest bank reconciliation. It needs your open invoices and bills with their due dates, and the payment history that measures days-to-pay. If you use credit cards, it needs the latest card statements. It asks how many days past due an invoice can be before it counts as at risk. It needs the payroll calendar, debt service, tax dates, the floor and the facility typed in, because no ledger holds them. Twelve months of cash account activity makes the result better.
Gives backThe skill gives back seven sheets. They are the 13-week forecast, the collection detail with each customer's days-to-pay and sample size, and the disbursement detail with the source of each payment. Then come the liquidity alerts, the sensitivities, the forecast-versus-actual tracker and a coverage sheet. It asks before it makes an Excel file.
NeverThe skill never draws on a facility, schedules a payment or defers anything. It never defaults the opening balance, the floor, the payroll amounts or the entity. It never puts payroll or a tax remittance on the lever list. It reads nothing before you answer its questions and say yes.
